content: Health personnel responsible for the distribution of misoprostol are already in place. Within an antenatal distribution program, misoprostol should ideally be provided to women during a third-trimester antenatal care visit, often as part of a safe delivery kit. This distribution must include clear and culturally appropriate instructions regarding its purpose, the correct dosage (400 or 600 micrograms for oral administration), the timing of its use, potential side effects and their management, and the recognition of danger signs. Women should also be informed about how to access health services, with an emphasis on the importance of delivering in a healthcare facility. In settings where antenatal distribution of misoprostol is being introduced, prospective research should prioritize evaluating the impact of these programs on maternal health outcomes and healthcare service utilization. This is critical to ensure the effectiveness of such interventions. In 2017, an estimated 295,000 women and adolescent girls died due to pregnancy and childbirth-related complications, with 99% of these deaths occurring in low-resource settings. Obstetric hemorrhage, particularly postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), accounts for over a quarter of all maternal deaths globally. In most low-income countries, PPH is the leading cause of maternal mortality. Improving access to safe and effective interventions to prevent PPH is therefore a critical priority for the World Health Organization (WHO) in achieving the targets of Sustainable Development Goal 3 (SDG 3), which focuses on health and well-being. International human rights law obligates states to ensure that women and adolescent girls survive pregnancy and childbirth as part of their sexual and reproductive health rights and their right to live a life of dignity. WHO envisions a world where every pregnant woman and newborn receives quality care throughout pregnancy, childbirth, and the postnatal period. To achieve this, skilled health personnel at all levels of the healthcare system must have access to appropriate medications and training in relevant procedures. Healthcare providers, managers, policymakers, and other stakeholders require up-to-date, evidence-based recommendations to guide clinical policies and practices, optimize care quality, and improve health outcomes. PPH is commonly defined as blood loss of 500 mL or more within 24 hours after birth and affects approximately 5% of women giving birth worldwide. Severe maternal complications, such as organ dysfunction or death, often result from significant blood loss that compromises maternal hemodynamic stability. Uterine atony is the most common cause of PPH and the leading cause of PPH-related maternal mortality globally. Other causes include genital tract trauma (e.g., vaginal or cervical lacerations, uterine rupture), retained placental tissue, or maternal bleeding disorders. While PPH can occur in any woman, certain factors increase the risk, including grand multiparity, prolonged labor, a history of PPH, multiple gestations, and anemia, which is a common aggravating factor. The majority of PPH-related complications can be prevented by using prophylactic uterotonics during the third stage of labor (the time between the delivery of the baby and the complete expulsion of the placenta). Misoprostol, a prostaglandin E1 analogue, is one such uterotonic. Although it is licensed for the prevention and treatment of gastric ulcers, it is widely used off-label as a uterotonic agent. Misoprostol is water-soluble, heat-stable, absorbed within 9–15 minutes, and has a half-life of approximately 20–40 minutes. Oral and sublingual routes offer rapid onset of action, while vaginal and rectal routes provide prolonged activity and greater bioavailability. WHO recommends misoprostol as a uterotonic option for PPH prevention, particularly in settings where oxytocin is unavailable. For women likely to give birth outside a healthcare facility, access to an effective uterotonic for PPH prevention or treatment is a significant challenge. This has led to the development and evaluation of advanced distribution strategies to ensure women have access to misoprostol after home or community births. These strategies may involve community-based distribution of misoprostol to traditional birth attendants, community health workers, or lay health workers who attend home or community births and are trained to administer misoprostol safely. In contexts where women give birth at home without skilled health personnel, advance distribution of misoprostol to pregnant women themselves during the last trimester for self-administration in the third stage of labor has emerged as a potential strategy to increase access to PPH prevention. WHO has established a new process for prioritizing and updating maternal and perinatal health recommendations. This process is overseen by the Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG), an international panel of independent experts. Recommendations are prioritized for updating based on changes or uncertainties in evidence regarding benefits, harms, values, acceptability, feasibility, equity, resource use, cost-effectiveness, or implementation factors. The updated recommendation on advance misoprostol distribution was developed following WHO's guideline development standards, including evidence synthesis, GRADE methodology, and input from a Guideline Development Group (GDG) composed of international experts and stakeholders. The updated recommendation supersedes the previous 2012 WHO recommendation on advance misoprostol distribution for PPH prevention. Its primary aim is to improve the quality of care and outcomes for women giving birth, particularly concerning PPH and its complications. These recommendations provide a foundation for sustainable implementation of advance misoprostol distribution strategies for PPH prevention. The target audience for this recommendation includes health professionals responsible for developing national and local healthcare guidelines and protocols, particularly those related to PPH prevention and treatment. It also includes midwives, nurses, general medical practitioners, obstetricians, maternal and child health program managers, and relevant staff in ministries of health and training institutions. Additionally, the recommendation is relevant to women giving birth in low-resource settings, professional societies involved in maternal care, non-governmental organizations promoting people-centered maternal care, and implementers of maternal and perinatal health programs. The recommendation was framed using the Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome (PICO) format to address whether advance misoprostol distribution to pregnant women for PPH prevention improves maternal outcomes compared to no advance distribution or usual care. The affected population includes all pregnant women in lowand middle-income settings. The recommendation was developed using standardized procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. This process involved identifying priority questions and critical outcomes, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, formulating the recommendation, and planning for dissemination, implementation, impact evaluation, and updating. In 2019, advance misoprostol distribution strategies were identified as a high priority for recommendation development due to new evidence on this intervention. Six main groups contributed to the process, including the Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG), WHO Steering Group, Guideline Development Group (GDG), Evidence Synthesis Group (ESG), external partners and observers, and the External Review Group (ERG). Each group played a specific role in evidence appraisal, recommendation formulation, and ensuring the clarity and contextual relevance of the final document.
